title: API Management with Apigee
bodyMarkdown:
# API Management with Apigee

Once services are consumed by partners, mobile apps, and other teams, you need a layer that authenticates callers, limits consumption, reshapes payloads, publishes documentation, and measures usage. On Google Cloud that layer is **Apigee**. The exam rarely asks how to write a policy; it asks whether you can match a requirement (per-partner limits, payload transformation, a self-service portal, monetization) to the right product and the right policy.

## Which API product do I pick?

Google Cloud has three API-facing options. The deciding factor is how much *management* the scenario needs.

| Need | Product | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Full API lifecycle: developer portal, API products, per-app quotas, mediation, analytics, monetization | **Apigee** | The enterprise answer; sits in front of any backend |
| Simple, serverless-style API front door with auth | **API Gateway** | OpenAPI 2.0 spec; backends are Cloud Run functions, Cloud Run, App Engine |
| OpenAPI or gRPC service with auth, API keys, quotas, and monitoring, via a proxy you deploy | **Cloud Endpoints** | ESPv2 (Envoy-based, recommended) or ESP (NGINX-based) |

[API Gateway](https://cloud.google.com/api-gateway/docs/about-api-gateway) defines an API as an OpenAPI 2.0 spec containing the backend URL, request and response formats, and the authentication mechanism. It supports API keys, Google authentication methods and service accounts, and Google ID tokens, and it tracks latency, traffic, and errors. It does not give you a developer portal, monetization, or payload mediation.

[Cloud Endpoints](https://cloud.google.com/endpoints/docs/openapi/about-cloud-endpoints) handles OpenAPI (2.0 and 3.x) and gRPC. You deploy the API config to Service Management and run **ESP** (NGINX-based, for existing users) or **ESPv2** (Envoy-based, recommended for new deployments) next to the backend. ESPv2 runs on GKE, Compute Engine, Kubernetes, App Engine standard, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions; ESP also supports App Engine flexible. It validates API keys, authenticates users, and supports quota configuration.

[Apigee](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/get-started/what-apigee) is the answer when the question mentions any of: a **developer portal**, **per-app or per-partner quotas**, **payload transformation**, **monetization (rate plans)**, **advanced analytics**, or **abuse detection**. It also supports OAuth2, API keys, SAML policies, and IAM-based authentication.

## Core Apigee concepts

- **API proxy**: the facade clients call. It has a **ProxyEndpoint** (faces clients) and a **TargetEndpoint** (faces the backend). Logic runs in [flows](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/fundamentals/understanding-apis-and-api-proxies): a **PreFlow** that executes before any conditional flows, conditional flows, and a **PostFlow**, on both the request and response paths.
- **Policy**: a configurable step attached to a flow location. Policies add security, rate limiting, caching, and transformation without changing the backend code.
- **API product**: a [bundle of API proxies and resources](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/publish/what-api-product) with quota limits, OAuth scopes, and an access level (public, private, or internal). It is the unit you publish and the unit of entitlement.
- **Developer and app**: a developer registers an app; the app receives credentials (API key, which is the OAuth client ID in OAuth terms) associated with one or more API products.

The runtime check ties these together: [VerifyAPIKey](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/reference/policies/verify-api-key-policy) ensures the key is valid, has not been revoked, and is approved to consume the specific resources in the API products attached to the app. The `status` of the app (for example approved or revoked) is exposed as a flow variable. Passing the key in a query parameter is allowed but a poor practice because query strings appear in logs and URLs; prefer a header.

## Rate limiting: Quota, SpikeArrest, and concurrent limits

This is the single most-tested Apigee distinction, so be precise.

| | **Quota** | **SpikeArrest** |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Business limit over a time window | Protect the backend from bursts |
| Example | 10,000 calls per month, or 1,000 per minute per partner | `12pm` or `5ps` |
| Scope | Counted per app, developer, API product, client ID, or any identifier you choose | Smooths traffic across the proxy (identifier optional) |
| Behavior | Counter persists until its window resets | Smooths: `5ps` becomes about one request every 200 ms |
| Over the limit | HTTP 429 | HTTP 429 (`SpikeArrestViolation`) |

The [Quota policy](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/reference/policies/quota-policy) lets you "limit apps to 1 request per minute, or to 10,000 requests per month." A single policy can keep many counters using the `<Identifier>` or `<Class>` elements, for example one per app or per developer. Three quota types control when counting starts and resets: `calendar` (explicit start time), `rollingwindow` (counts requests in the preceding interval), and `flexi` (the counter starts at the app's first request). If you set no type, the counter resets at the start of the minute, hour, day, week, or month. Quota counters are scoped to the API proxy that contains the policy and are not shared across proxies, even within one API product, and all Quota times are UTC. The documentation explicitly says not to use Quota to shield against overall spikes.

The [SpikeArrest policy](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/reference/policies/spike-arrest-policy) takes a `<Rate>` in `ps` (per second) or `pm` (per minute). Via smoothing, `5ps` is enforced as at most one request per 200 ms (1000/5); `12pm` is one request per 5 seconds. Exceeding it returns 429. Apigee also has a **ConcurrentRateLimit** policy for limiting simultaneous connections to the backend.

Rule of thumb: **Quota answers "how much may this partner consume?"; SpikeArrest answers "how do I keep a burst from hurting the backend?"** Real designs use both, and the [rate-limiting overview](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/develop/rate-limiting) lists a 429 as the response for either.

## Mediation and other policies

The [XMLtoJSON policy](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/reference/policies/xml-json-policy) converts XML to JSON, and is attached to the response flow. A typical mediation pairs a JSONtoXML policy on the request flow with XMLtoJSON on the response flow, so a JSON API can front a backend that only speaks XML. You can also execute the pair conditionally to serve whichever format the client prefers.

Other commonly referenced policies: **OAuthV2** (token issuance and verification), **AssignMessage** and **ExtractVariables** (shape messages and read values), **ServiceCallout** (call another service mid-flow), and **DataCapture** (capture custom analytics data). Policy fault handling uses fault rules and flow variables so you can return clean error payloads.

## Portal, analytics, and monetization

- **Integrated portal**: publish API products, show OpenAPI-based documentation, let developers register apps and get API keys, with configurable account creation and approval. See the [portal documentation](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/publish/portal/publish-apis).
- **Analytics**: [dashboards](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/analytics/analytics-services-overview) for proxy performance, error codes, latency, cache performance, developer engagement, app-level traffic, and API product usage; custom reports; export to BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
- **Monetization**: rate plans for API products and prepaid balances.

## Versioning and deprecating an API

Apigee documents the mechanisms; the versioning policy itself is API design guidance (the [proxy best-practices page](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/fundamentals/best-practices-api-proxy-design-and-development) defers to Apigee's API design e-book). The mechanisms that matter:

- **Revision is not version.** The [proxy documentation](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/fundamentals/understanding-apis-and-api-proxies) warns not to confuse the version of an API (the public interface) with the revision of a proxy (an internal number for a configuration). The two are unrelated, and the revision number is totally opaque to apps. Revisions are sequentially numbered, so a rollback is deploying a previous revision.
- **A new revision replaces the old one.** When you [deploy](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/deploy/ui-deploy-new) a new revision without changing its base path into an environment where the proxy is already deployed, the previous revision is undeployed. Revisions therefore cannot give you v1 and v2 side by side.
- **Version and base path travel together.** Each proxy has a base path, so two major versions run in parallel as two proxies on different base paths, such as `/v1/orders` and `/v2/orders`.
- **Analytics is per proxy and per app.** The [analytics reference](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/analytics/analytics-reference) lists the Proxy (`apiproxy`), Proxy base path and Developer app dimensions, so a custom report can show which apps still call the old proxy.

The design guidance built on those mechanisms:

1. Put the **major version in the base path** and give **each major version its own proxy**.
2. **Additive changes need no new version:** a new optional field or a new endpoint. A **breaking change** needs one: a removed or renamed field, a changed type, a new required parameter or changed semantics.
3. **Announce a deprecation window** with a retirement date, run both proxies in parallel through it, and use per-proxy, per-app analytics to find stragglers before you undeploy the old proxy.
4. **Traffic splitting is a rollout tool.** Sending a share of calls to a new implementation of the same contract is not versioning, because the client cannot choose it.

Since an API product bundles proxies, adding the new proxy to the product the partners' apps already hold keeps their credentials valid, while a separate product lets you price or limit the versions differently.

## Deployment models

Apigee is offered as a fully managed service on Google Cloud, and as [Apigee hybrid](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/hybrid/latest/what-is-hybrid): a management plane hosted and maintained by Google (UI, management API, analytics) plus a **runtime plane you install and operate on a supported Kubernetes platform**, in your data center, Google Cloud, or both. Choose hybrid when compliance, latency, or data-residency requirements force the runtime onto your premises or another cloud; choose the managed offering otherwise.

## Architecture guidance

- Authenticate at the proxy edge with VerifyAPIKey or OAuthV2; never rely on the backend alone, and never expose the backend directly.
- Put a **Quota** keyed on the app or developer to stop one partner from starving others, and add **SpikeArrest** to protect the backend from bursts.
- Mediate payloads in the proxy so client and backend formats evolve independently.
- Package proxies into API products, publish through the portal, and review analytics to manage the API as a product.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Choosing API Gateway or Endpoints when the scenario needs a portal, monetization, or per-partner products.** Those are Apigee capabilities.
- **Using SpikeArrest as a business quota.** It smooths bursts; it does not count a monthly allowance per partner.
- **Using Quota for burst protection.** The docs say not to; use SpikeArrest.
- **Assuming one Quota is shared across all proxies in an API product.** Counters are scoped to the proxy that contains the policy.
- **Hardcoding IP allow-lists or credentials in the target endpoint or a JavaScript policy.** Use VerifyAPIKey or OAuthV2 against registered apps and API products.
- **Putting the API key in the query string.** It leaks into logs and browser history.
- **Relying on Cloud CDN or Cloud Armor as an API product.** They help with delivery and edge protection but do not provide app registration, entitlement, or per-app quotas.
- **Choosing hybrid by default.** Hybrid moves runtime operations to you; use it only when residency or on-premises requirements demand it.
- **Using proxy revisions as partner-visible versions.** Revision numbers are internal and opaque to apps, and a new revision replaces the deployed one.
- **Shipping a breaking change under the same version.** Partners break on the day you deploy; publish a new major version and a deprecation window.
- **Retiring the old version on a date nobody measured against.** Check per-app analytics for remaining callers first.

## Exam tips

- **"Portal plus per-app quotas plus analytics" means Apigee.** If the requirement lists developer portal, key issuance, monetization, or mediation, API Gateway and Cloud Endpoints are the wrong tier.
- **Quota is business, SpikeArrest is protection.** "No partner may exceed N calls per minute" is Quota keyed per app; "smooth out sudden bursts" is SpikeArrest.
- **Both rate limiters return 429** when exceeded; a 429 does not tell you which policy fired.
- **VerifyAPIKey checks entitlement, not just validity.** It confirms the key is valid, not revoked, and approved for the API product being called.
- **Mediation lives in the proxy.** XMLtoJSON on the response flow (paired with JSONtoXML on the request) lets modern clients use JSON against an XML backend without touching the backend.
- **API product is the unit of publishing and entitlement.** Apps get keys tied to API products, and products carry quota, scopes, and access level.
- **Versioning: major version in the base path, one proxy per major version.** Run both through an announced deprecation window and watch per-proxy, per-app analytics before retiring the old one.
- **Revision is not version.** A proxy revision is internal deployment history, opaque to apps; additive changes need no new version and traffic splitting is a rollout tool, not versioning.
- **Hybrid means you run the runtime plane.** Google hosts the management plane; the customer operates the Kubernetes runtime.
- **API Gateway uses OpenAPI 2.0 and serverless backends.** Cloud Endpoints uses ESPv2 on your compute; neither offers a developer portal.
